templates.name: Main idea, informational study report (incl. explainer and scholar-argument passages)

items.passage: Larvae of the tobacco hornworm moth consume wild tobacco, whose leaves contain the neurotoxin nicotine. Biologist Pavan Kumar and colleagues determined that an enzyme produced in the larval midgut, CYP6B46, transfers a small proportion of ingested nicotine into the hemolymph (the insect equivalent of blood), from which it is exhaled through spiracles, respiratory openings along the body. Larvae feeding on tobacco plants engineered to suppress the larvae’s production of this enzyme were preferentially consumed by wolf spiders, though big-eyed bugs, another predator, displayed no such preference.
items.stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about the larvae that produced less CYP6B46?
options: They likely carried more of the nicotine they ate in their hemolymph than unaltered larvae did, which made them more appealing to wolf spiders.
They likely exhaled less nicotine than unaltered larvae did, which left them more exposed to all of the predators that hunt hornworm larvae.
They likely gained less protection against wolf spiders from the nicotine they ate, because less of that nicotine reached the air around them.
They likely were preferred by wolf spiders because they took in less of the nicotine in tobacco leaves than unaltered larvae did.
items.explanation: The text says that CYP6B46 moves some of the nicotine the larvae eat into their hemolymph, from which it is exhaled, and that larvae with less of the enzyme were eaten by wolf spiders more readily even though they still fed on tobacco. Together these facts suggest that the nicotine those larvae ate protected them less against wolf spiders because less of it was released into the air.

A.why_wrong: Wolf spiders did prefer these larvae, but the enzyme is what moves ingested nicotine into the hemolymph, so larvae making less of it would carry less nicotine there, not more.

B.why_wrong: Exhaling less nicotine is a fair inference, but big-eyed bugs showed no preference for the altered larvae, so the larvae were not more exposed to all predators.

D.why_wrong: Wolf spiders did prefer these larvae, but the larvae still fed on tobacco, and the enzyme acts on nicotine already eaten; the text never says they took in less of it.

sources.what: Kumar, Pandit, Steppuhn and Baldwin, PNAS 2014: CYP6B46 moves ingested nicotine from the midgut into the hemolymph and larvae exhale it; wolf spiders preferred CYP6B46-silenced larvae fed on plants making dsRNA; big-eyed bugs and antlion larvae were insensitive

items.notes: Natural science (chemical ecology). P1: the enzyme moves ingested nicotine to the hemolymph, where it is exhaled; P2: larvae with less enzyme, still eating tobacco, were preferred by wolf spiders; unstated conclusion: eating nicotine alone did not protect them. Spiracles glossed in place; plant-mediated RNAi glossed as plants engineered to suppress the enzyme. Ian T. Baldwin (senior author) left unnamed because our inferences.S9.hard.w2b1_07 names him for a different coyote-tobacco study (flower timing).

fixes: hardened to band 6: A was a bare wrong mechanism and D an invented repellent; both now keep the true wolf-spider preference and fail on the mechanism (A reverses which way the enzyme moves nicotine, D swaps exhalation for intake); re-solved blind, C only

band7.why: Planned band 6 (every Central Ideas hard cell is 6). Two links (less enzyme means less nicotine exhaled; wolf spiders alone preferred those larvae, so the nicotine protected them less); key paraphrased (reached the air). After hardening all three distractors are partly right: A CON-half (reversed mechanism), B overextended to all predators, D TWI (intake for exhalation). Options 22 to 24 words, no stance word or aside, so strong band 6.

items.passage: Approximately 336 meters from the entrance of Bruniquel Cave in southwestern France, in a chamber accessible only through a lengthy, narrow passage, roughly 400 fragments of broken stalagmites were deliberately arranged into two large circular structures and several smaller accumulations. Many of the fragments bear evidence of exposure to fire. In 2016 archaeologist Jacques Jaubert and colleagues dated the thin layers of calcite that had accumulated on the fragments since their placement, obtaining an age of approximately 176,500 years, a period when Neanderthals were the only humans known to have inhabited the region.
items.stem: Based on the text, what can most reasonably be concluded about the structures in Bruniquel Cave?
options: They were likely built no later than about 176,500 years ago, since the dated calcite formed only after the pieces had been arranged.
They were likely built about 176,500 years ago, when the stalagmites that were later broken into pieces first began to grow in the cave.
They were likely built by people who reached the chamber through its long, narrow passage, though not until long after the dated calcite had formed.
They were likely built after the fires that marked the pieces had burned out, since the traces of fire lie beneath the dated calcite.
items.explanation: The text says that the dated calcite grew over the pieces after they were set in place and that this calcite is about 176,500 years old. Because the arrangement had to exist before the calcite could form on it, the structures were most likely built no later than about 176,500 years ago.

B.why_wrong: The date comes from calcite that grew after the pieces were placed, not from the time the stalagmites themselves began to grow, which would have been much earlier.

C.why_wrong: The builders would have reached the chamber through the narrow passage, but the dated calcite accumulated on the fragments after they were placed, so the structures could not have been built after it formed.

D.why_wrong: The text says many pieces bear traces of fire but never says where those traces lie in relation to the calcite or when the fires burned.

sources.what: Bruniquel Cave (Jaubert, Verheyden, Genty et al., Nature 2016): about 400 broken stalagmite pieces arranged in rings about a third of a kilometre (336 m) from the entrance, reached by a narrow passage, with signs of burning; dated from calcite that formed after the stalagmites were broken off, about 176,500 years ago; Neanderthals the only humans in the region then

items.notes: Archaeology. P1: calcite grew over the pieces after placement; P2: that calcite is about 176,500 years old; unstated conclusion: the date is a minimum age (no later than). Nature abstract: 336 m from the entrance, age 176.5 +/- 2.1 ka from stalagmite regrowths.

fixes: hardened to band 6: C (calcite thickness) had no foothold in the text; now a true first clause (reached through the narrow passage) with the order of building and calcite reversed; re-solved blind, A only

band7.why: Planned band 6. Key needs the minimum-age step (calcite formed after placement, so the date is a ceiling on building time); distractors TWI (wrong dated material), CON-half (order reversed), UNS (fire traces under calcite), each with a true foothold after the fix. Options 23 to 25 words; no stance word, so band 6.

items.passage: In 1978 artist Mónica Mayer distributed pink cards on the streets of Mexico City, inviting women to complete the sentence “As a woman, what I dislike most about the city is . . .” She then pinned the returned cards in rows on a clothesline, an object associated with the domestic labor traditionally assigned to women, and exhibited the installation, El Tendedero (The Clothesline), at the city’s Museum of Modern Art. Numerous responses described sexual harassment encountered on streets or on public transportation.
items.stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about El Tendedero?
options: It likely drew many responses about harassment because the cards Mayer handed out asked women specifically to describe harassment they had faced in the city.
It likely gathered more responses about public transportation than about any other part of city life that the participating women disliked.
It likely suggested that the women’s chief complaints concerned housework rather than city life, since their answers were hung on a clothesline.
It likely showed that harassment in public was a widely shared experience by displaying many women’s separate answers side by side.
items.explanation: The text says that Mayer collected answers from many women, that she displayed the cards together on a clothesline, and that numerous answers described sexual harassment on streets or public transportation. Shown side by side, so many separate accounts of the same problem would most likely reveal harassment as an experience that many women shared.

A.why_wrong: Many responses did describe harassment, but the cards asked a general question, what women disliked most about the city, so the harassment accounts came from the women themselves, not from the wording of the cards.

B.why_wrong: The text says many responses described harassment on the street or on public transportation; it never says which subject drew the most responses.

C.why_wrong: The clothesline is linked to domestic labor, but the cards asked what women disliked about the city, and many answers described harassment on streets and public transportation, not housework.

sources.what: Monica Mayer, El Tendedero (The Clothesline), 1978: women asked to complete As a woman, what I dislike most about the city is... on pink slips, mounted on a clothesline that refers to daily work considered women's work, first shown at the Museo de Arte Moderno, Mexico City
many responses described sexual harassment, especially on public transportation; cards handed out on the streets

items.notes: Arts (participatory feminist art). P1: many women's separate answers displayed together; P2: many described harassment; unstated conclusion: the display revealed a shared experience. No count of cards given (sources disagree: 800 invited vs hundreds handed out).

fixes: hardened to band 6: A (Mayer’s own complaints) and C (city officials) each fell to one fact; A now keeps the true harassment responses but credits them to the card wording, C keeps the true clothesline link but concludes the complaints were about housework; explanation aligned; re-solved blind, D only

band7.why: Planned band 6. Two links (many separate answers shown together; numerous ones on harassment) to an unstated conclusion; after hardening A (card wording), B (invented comparison) and C (clothesline read as housework) each keep a true detail. Options 21 to 25 words; no stance word, so band 6.

items.passage:
The following text is from Juan Valera’s 1874 novel Pepita Ximenez (translated in 1886). Luis, a young man studying to become a priest, is describing Pepita, a young widow whom his father hopes to marry, in a letter to his uncle.

It is evident that she takes great care of her hands, and is, perhaps, to a certain extent, vain of their beauty and whiteness, as well as of her rose-colored and polished nails; but if this be so, it is to be pardoned to the weakness of the flesh; and indeed, if I remember aright, I think that St. Theresa, in her youth, had this same species of vanity, which did not prevent her, however, from becoming a great saint.

In truth, I can understand, even though I do not excuse, this little piece of vanity.
items.stem: Based on the text, how does Luis regard Pepita’s care for her hands?
options: He condemns it as a weakness of the flesh that will prevent her from ever becoming as devout as St. Theresa was.
He claims not to excuse it, though he has just described it as a forgivable weakness that a saint also had.
He regards it as a sign of the same holiness that later made St. Theresa a great saint.
He finds it understandable, but he believes that it makes her an unsuitable wife for his father.
items.explanation: Luis first says that Pepita’s vanity about her hands “is to be pardoned to the weakness of the flesh” and notes that St. Theresa had “this same species of vanity” yet became a great saint. He then declares that he does “not excuse” this vanity. Choice B captures this: he refuses to excuse the vanity right after presenting it as a forgivable weakness that a saint shared.

A.recipe: surface reading that contradicts the text
A.why_wrong: Luis notes that the same vanity did not prevent St. Theresa from becoming a great saint, so he does not say it will keep Pepita from being devout.

C.why_wrong: Luis does compare Pepita with St. Theresa, but he says the saint’s vanity “did not prevent her” from becoming a saint; he presents it as a weakness, not as a sign of holiness.

D.why_wrong: Luis does say he can understand the vanity, but nothing in the text suggests he thinks it makes Pepita unsuitable to marry his father.

sources.what: Project Gutenberg 30236, Pepita Ximenez by Juan Valera, D. Appleton and Company 1886 (no translator credited); text copied exactly, trimmed at sentence boundaries; novel first published in Spanish in 1874

items.notes: Literary irony variant of T6: the narrator says one thing (does not excuse) that his own preceding sentence undercuts (it is to be pardoned). Luis has taken minor orders and writes letters to his uncle, the Dean; his father Don Pedro courts the widow Pepita.

fixes: excerpt checked against Project Gutenberg 30236: exact, contiguous

key paraphrased (forgivable weakness that a saint also had) while keeping the stance word excuse; C was a flat contradiction, now a half-true comparison with St. Theresa (holiness instead of a vanity the saint overcame); explanation aligned; re-solved blind, B only

band7.why: Planned band 6. Literary irony variant of T6 with the band-7 key frame (claims A, though B), but the stance word excuse is quoted in the text and the contradiction sits in two adjacent sentences, so it is reachable in one comparison. After the fix all three distractors partly right (weakness of the flesh, St. Theresa, understandable). Strong band 6.

items.passage: Philosophical discussions of silencing frequently concentrate on listeners who refuse to recognize a speaker as a credible source of knowledge. Philosopher Kristie Dotson has identified a less conspicuous practice, testimonial smothering, in which speakers truncate their own testimony so that it contains only what their audience appears capable of understanding. Such self-censorship might seem attributable to the speaker’s preference alone, but Dotson traces it to specific conditions: the testimony is risky to offer, and the audience has demonstrated, through a pernicious ignorance, an inability to receive that testimony competently.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Dotson describes a form of silencing that can look self-imposed, arguing that it is a response to risk and to an audience whose harmful ignorance limits what it can understand.
Dotson argues that speakers who cut short their own testimony usually do so because they have misjudged how much their audiences are able to understand.
Dotson identifies a form of silencing that is harder to detect than listeners’ refusal to treat speakers as credible and is therefore more damaging to speakers.
Dotson contends that testimonial smothering occurs whenever testimony is risky to offer, regardless of whether the audience has shown that it can understand that testimony.
items.explanation: The text explains that in testimonial smothering speakers shorten their own testimony, which may look like their own choice, but that Dotson traces it to two conditions: the testimony is risky, and the audience has shown, because of a harmful ignorance, that it cannot take the testimony up. Choice A joins both parts: the silencing looks self-imposed but responds to risk and to the audience’s harmful ignorance.

B.why_wrong: The text says the audience has shown it cannot take the testimony up, so the speaker has not simply misjudged the audience.

C.why_wrong: The text calls smothering less visible but never says it is more damaging than listeners’ refusal to treat speakers as credible.

D.why_wrong: The text gives two conditions, and one of them is that the audience has shown it cannot competently take up the testimony.

sources.what: Kristie Dotson, Tracking Epistemic Violence, Tracking Practices of Silencing, Hypatia 26(2), 2011, pp. 236-257: testimonial quieting vs testimonial smothering

Dotson's definition and three conditions quoted with page numbers (speaker truncates testimony; content unsafe and risky; audience demonstrates testimonial incompetence; incompetence follows from pernicious ignorance)

items.notes: Humanities (philosophy, social epistemology). Scholar-argument T1: the governing claim is spread over S2 and S3, so the key joins the definition and the conditions. Pernicious ignorance rendered as harmful ignorance; testimonial competence as competently take up.

band7.why: Planned band 6. Main idea joins the concession (looks self-imposed) and both conditions; key paraphrased (harmful ignorance); distractors TWI (misjudged audience), CMP (more damaging), CON-half (drops the audience condition), all partly right. Options 22 to 30 words against a band-7 main-idea median of 34, no stance word, so strong band 6.

items.passage: Between 1837 and 1863, numerous US states permitted almost anyone to establish a bank and issue paper currency, provided the bank deposited government bonds with state authorities as security for its notes. Historians long characterized this “free banking” era as one dominated by fraudulent wildcat bankers who circulated notes and then disappeared, leaving the public holding worthless paper. But when economists Arthur Rolnick and Warren Weber examined the records of free banks in several states, they determined that most failures coincided with substantial declines in the prices of the bonds securing the notes rather than resulting from fraud.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Although falling bond prices weakened many free banks, Rolnick and Weber found that most of the bankers whose banks failed had vanished before their notes lost value.
Although free banking let almost anyone open a bank, few people did so in the states Rolnick and Weber studied because depositing bonds with the state was costly.
Although historians have described free banks as fraudulent, Rolnick and Weber found that those banks failed less often than banks in later periods did.
Although free banks have been remembered for fraud, research suggests that most of those that failed did so because the assets backing their notes lost value.
items.explanation: The text says historians long portrayed free banking as an era of fraudulent wildcat bankers, but Rolnick and Weber found that most failures came when the bonds backing the banks’ notes dropped in price rather than from fraud. Choice D states both the old view and the revision, with the bonds described as the assets backing the notes.

A.why_wrong: Rolnick and Weber found that most failures came from falling bond prices rather than fraud, which goes against the image of bankers vanishing with the public’s money.

B.why_wrong: The text never says how many people opened banks or that depositing bonds was too costly.

C.why_wrong: The text never compares the failure rate of free banks with that of banks in later periods.

sources.what: Rolnick and Weber, The Causes of Free Bank Failures (Minneapolis Fed staff report 1982, J. Monetary Economics 1984): periods of falling bond prices correspond to the periods with most free bank failures; the data do not support the view that fraud caused the failures

items.notes: Social science (economic history, historiography). View then correction: wildcat-fraud image, then the bond-price explanation. Free banking era 1837 (Michigan) to 1863 (National Banking Act); notes backed by state or federal bonds deposited with the state. Replaces the earlier run's Frachetti Silk Road subject (Silk Road already used elsewhere).

band7.why: Planned band 6. All four options in one Although frame with true first clauses; distractors CON-half (keeps the fraud view), UNS (costly bonds), CMP (later banks); key paraphrased (assets backing their notes). Correction signalled by a plain But, not a stance word, so band 6.

items.passage:
The following text is Hazel Hall’s 1921 poem “Instruction.”

My hands that guide a needle
In their turn are led
Relentlessly and deftly
As a needle leads a thread.

Other hands are teaching
My needle; when I sew
I feel the cool, thin fingers
Of hands I do not know.

They urge my needle onward,
They smooth my seams, until
The worry of my stitches
Smothers in their skill.

All the tired women,
Who sewed their lives away,
Speak in my deft fingers
As I sew to-day.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: The speaker is being taught to sew by an older relative, whose cool, thin fingers guide the speaker’s hands as the speaker works.
The speaker senses that the skill of many women who sewed in the past lives on in the speaker’s hands, easing the work.
The speaker worries that, like the tired women of earlier times, the speaker will spend a whole life at work that brings little reward.
The speaker feels pressured by unseen hands that relentlessly drive the needle, leaving the speaker anxious about every stitch.
items.explanation: The speaker feels unseen “hands I do not know” leading the needle, urging it on and smoothing the seams until the speaker’s worry “smothers in their skill.” The last stanza names these hands as “all the tired women, / Who sewed their lives away,” whose skill now speaks in the speaker’s fingers. Choice B states this idea.

A.why_wrong: The guiding fingers belong to “hands I do not know,” later identified as the many women who sewed in the past, not a living relative giving lessons.

C.why_wrong: The speaker’s worry “smothers in their skill,” so the poem shows the past women easing the speaker’s worry, not a fear of the future.

D.why_wrong: Unseen hands do lead the needle “relentlessly,” but they smooth the seams until “the worry of my stitches / Smothers in their skill,” so they ease the speaker’s worry rather than cause it.

sources.what: Hazel Hall, Curtains (John Lane Company, 1921), poem Instruction, p. 100; copied exactly from the scan (two scans agree; also printed in Poetry, May 1921)

items.notes: Poem, extended figure (unseen hands guiding the needle carried into the general claim that past women's skill lives in the speaker). Hall was a needleworker in Portland, Oregon. Not used in any official item or ours.

fixes: poem checked against the archive.org scan of Curtains (1921), p. 100: exact

key paraphrased away from “sewed their lives away” (skill of past women lives on in the speaker’s hands); D was a flat contradiction, now a half-true tonal misreading (relentless unseen hands leave the speaker anxious, against “Smothers in their skill”); explanation aligned; re-solved blind, B only

band7.why: Planned band 6. One extended figure (unseen hands leading the needle) carried into a general claim; after the fix the key is paraphrased and distractors are LIT (a living relative), TON (fear of a wasted life) and CON-half (relentless hands cause worry), each with a foothold in the poem. Options 19 to 24 words, so band 6.

items.passage:
The following text is from Multatuli’s 1860 novel Max Havelaar (translated by Baron Alphonse Nahuijs in 1868). The narrator, Batavus Droogstoppel, has decided to write a book.

I am a coffee-broker, and live at No. 37 Laurier Canal, Amsterdam. I am not accustomed to write novels or works of that kind; therefore it took me a long time before I could resolve to order a few extra quires of paper and begin this book, which you, dear reader, have just taken in hand, and which you must finish, whether you are a coffee-broker or anything else. Not only that I never wrote anything that resembled a novel, but I even do not like to read such things, because I am a man of business.
items.stem: According to the text, why did it take the narrator a long time to begin his book?
options: He had to save money before he could buy the paper he needed.
His work as a coffee-broker left him little time for writing.
He is not in the habit of writing novels or similar works.
He doubted that readers who are not coffee-brokers would finish it.
items.explanation: The narrator says, “I am not accustomed to write novels or works of that kind; therefore it took me a long time” to begin the book. Choice C restates this reason.

A.why_wrong: The narrator mentions ordering “a few extra quires of paper,” but he never says he lacked the money for it.

B.why_wrong: Being “a man of business” is the reason he gives for not liking to read novels, not for taking a long time to start writing.

D.why_wrong: The narrator tells readers they must finish the book “whether you are a coffee-broker or anything else”; he does not express doubt about them.

sources.what: Project Gutenberg 70128, Max Havelaar, or the Coffee Auctions of the Dutch Trading Company by Multatuli, translated by Baron Alphonse Nahuijs (Edinburgh: Edmonston and Douglas, 1868), chapter 1; copied exactly. Novel first published in Dutch in 1860.

items.notes: Literary explicit detail. The narrator Batavus Droogstoppel is a coffee broker of Laurier Canal (named later in chapter 1: my name is Batavus). Two reasons sit side by side: not accustomed to writing (the answer) and being a man of business (why he dislikes reading novels), which B borrows.

fixes: excerpt checked against Project Gutenberg 70128: exact

items.passage: For a female moorland hawker dragonfly (Aeshna juncea), a single mating can fertilize all of her eggs, so continued pursuit by males offers her no reproductive benefit. Males nevertheless chase females persistently. While conducting fieldwork in the Swiss Alps, ecologist Rassim Khelifa noticed that females pursued in this way occasionally crash-dived to the ground and remained motionless until their pursuers departed. Of the 27 females he observed feigning death in this manner, 21 successfully escaped, a finding Khelifa reported in the journal Ecology in 2017.
items.stem: According to the text, what did Khelifa observe about the female moorland hawkers that feigned death?
options: Most of them managed to evade the males that were pursuing them.
Most of them were injured when they crash-dived to the ground.
They did so only after they had finished laying all of their eggs.
They attracted fewer males than females that hid in vegetation did.
items.explanation: The text says that of the 27 females Khelifa saw feigning death, 21 “successfully escaped.” Choice A restates this result.

B.why_wrong: The text never says the females were hurt by the fall.

C.why_wrong: The text mentions that one mating can fertilize all of a female’s eggs, but it never says when the females laid their eggs.

D.why_wrong: The text says nothing about females hiding in vegetation or about how many males different females attracted.

sources.what: Khelifa, Faking death to avoid male coercion: extreme sexual conflict resolution in a dragonfly, Ecology 98 (2017): moorland hawker females crash-dive and lie motionless when chased; 27 of 31 surveyed females did so and 21 escaped; one mating fertilizes all eggs

items.notes: Natural science (behavioral ecology). Counts vary between outlets (27 of 31 or 35 feigned death; 21 escaped); the passage gives the 21 of 27 that most outlets report.

items.passage: Roughly 1,500 years ago, builders in China began adding a soup made from sticky rice to lime mortar, and structures built with the mixture, including tombs, pagodas, and city walls, have proved remarkably durable. Analyzing samples of this mortar, chemist Bingjian Zhang and colleagues identified amylopectin, a carbohydrate in the rice, as the source of its strength: amylopectin functions as an inhibitor, regulating the growth of the calcium carbonate crystals that form as lime hardens and thereby producing a compact microstructure. The researchers also concluded that the mortar is well suited to restoring historic masonry.
items.stem: According to the text, what role does amylopectin play in sticky rice–lime mortar?
options: It makes the mortar compatible with historic masonry that was originally built without any rice.
It speeds up the rate at which the lime in the mortar hardens.
It replaces the calcium carbonate that lime would otherwise produce.
It limits how calcium carbonate crystals grow, giving the mortar a dense structure.
items.explanation: The text says that amylopectin acts as an inhibitor that regulates the growth of the calcium carbonate crystals that form as lime hardens, producing a compact microstructure. Choice D restates this role.

A.why_wrong: The text says the researchers found the mortar suitable for restoring historic masonry, but it does not say amylopectin makes the mortar match masonry built without rice.

B.why_wrong: The text says amylopectin controls crystal growth; it never says it makes lime harden faster.

C.why_wrong: The calcium carbonate crystals still form; amylopectin regulates their growth rather than replacing them.

sources.what: Yang, Zhang and Ma, Study of sticky rice-lime mortar technology for the restoration of historical masonry construction, Accounts of Chemical Research 2010; ScienceDaily summary: developed about 1,500 years ago, used in tombs, pagodas and city walls; amylopectin acts as an inhibitor controlling calcium carbonate crystal growth, giving a compact microstructure; suitable for restoration

items.notes: Technology and engineering (materials chemistry, conservation). Bingjian Zhang led the research group (Yang Fuwei first author).

items.passage: Most mammals avoid chili peppers because capsaicin, the compound responsible for their pungency, activates TRPV1, a receptor protein in sensory neurons that signals painful heat. The Chinese tree shrew, however, readily consumes the fruit of Piper boehmeriaefolium, a pepper plant that produces a capsaicin-like compound. Examining the shrew’s version of TRPV1, researchers at the Kunming Institute of Zoology identified a single amino acid substitution that substantially reduces the receptor’s sensitivity to such compounds, and they propose that the shrew’s diet may have favored this mutation.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Researchers found that the Chinese tree shrew is less sensitive to pain than other mammals are because it lacks the TRPV1 receptor entirely.
Researchers found that a small genetic difference may explain how the Chinese tree shrew can eat a pungent plant that most mammals avoid.
Piper boehmeriaefolium produces a capsaicin-like compound in order to discourage Chinese tree shrews from eating its fruit.
Researchers found that eating pungent fruit gradually makes the TRPV1 receptors of individual Chinese tree shrews less sensitive.
items.explanation: The text explains that most mammals avoid pungent plants because compounds like capsaicin activate TRPV1, that the Chinese tree shrew nonetheless eats a pungent pepper plant, and that researchers found a single amino acid change that makes the shrew’s TRPV1 much less sensitive. Choice B joins these points: a small genetic difference may explain the shrew’s unusual diet.

A.why_wrong: The researchers studied the shrew’s own version of TRPV1, so the shrew has the receptor; one amino acid in it differs.

C.why_wrong: The text never says why the plant produces the compound, and the shrews readily eat the fruit.

D.why_wrong: The text describes a mutation that the shrews’ diet may have favored over generations, not a change in each shrew during its life.

sources.what: Han et al., Molecular mechanism of the tree shrew's insensitivity to spiciness, PLoS Biology 2018 (Kunming Institute of Zoology): a single point mutation in tree shrew TRPV1 lowers sensitivity to capsaicinoids; Piper boehmeriaefolium, which produces the capsaicin analog Cap2, may have driven selection

items.notes: Natural science (molecular physiology, evolution). The earlier run's claim line says 2022; the paper is 2018, and the passage gives no year.

items.passage: In a series of experiments, psychologist David Rosenbaum and colleagues asked participants to walk down an alley, pick up one of two buckets positioned along it, and carry that bucket to the alley’s end. The researchers anticipated that participants would select the bucket nearer the endpoint, since doing so would minimize the distance it had to be carried. Instead, most participants chose the bucket closer to themselves, carrying it farther. Rosenbaum termed this tendency to complete a subgoal as quickly as possible, even at the expense of extra physical effort, “pre-crastination.”
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Researchers found that people carrying objects generally choose whatever route requires the least physical effort.
Rosenbaum showed that people who pre-crastinate complete their tasks more efficiently than people who delay them.
Research suggests that people often hurry to finish part of a task even when doing so requires additional effort.
Most of the participants picked up the bucket closer to themselves because they misunderstood the instructions.
items.explanation: The text describes an experiment in which most participants picked up the bucket closest to them and carried it farther than necessary, and it says Rosenbaum calls this tendency to complete a subgoal quickly, even with extra effort, pre-crastination. Choice C states this finding in general terms.

A.why_wrong: Most participants chose the bucket that had to be carried farther, which required more effort, not less.

B.why_wrong: The text never compares people who pre-crastinate with people who procrastinate or measures efficiency.

D.why_wrong: The text gives no sign that participants misunderstood the task; it presents their choice as a tendency the researchers named.

sources.what: Rosenbaum, Gong and Potts, Pre-crastination: hastening subgoal completion at the expense of extra physical effort, Psychological Science 2014; APS release: participants chose the bucket closer to the start and carried it farther

items.notes: Social science (cognitive psychology). Rosenbaum's definition: the hastening of subgoal completion, even at the expense of extra physical effort.

items.passage: Kinuyo Tanaka was already among Japan’s most celebrated film actresses, having starred in such productions as Kenji Mizoguchi’s The Life of Oharu (1952), when she directed her first feature, Love Letter, in 1953. With that film she became only the second woman to direct a feature in Japan. Over the following nine years she directed five more features, including Forever a Woman (1955), a portrait of a woman poet confronting a terminal illness, and The Wandering Princess (1960), about a Japanese noblewoman who married into the family of China’s last emperor.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Tanaka, already a renowned actress, became a pioneering film director whose films often centered on women’s lives.
Tanaka gave up acting in 1953 so that she could concentrate entirely on directing feature films of her own.
Tanaka directed The Life of Oharu shortly before she became one of Japan’s best-known actresses.
The films Tanaka directed drew larger audiences than the films she had made with Mizoguchi.
items.explanation: The text says that Tanaka was already a celebrated actress when, in 1953, she became only the second woman to direct a feature film in Japan, and that she went on to direct films about a woman poet and a noblewoman. Choice A sums up her pioneering move into directing and the women at the center of her films.

B.why_wrong: The text never says Tanaka stopped acting when she began directing.

C.why_wrong: Tanaka starred in The Life of Oharu, which Mizoguchi directed; she did not direct it.

D.why_wrong: The text never discusses the size of the audiences for any of Tanaka’s films.

sources.what: Kinuyo Tanaka: star of Mizoguchi films including The Life of Oharu (1952); directed Love Letter (1953), the second Japanese woman film director after Tazuko Sakane; six features 1953 to 1962 including Forever a Woman (1955, about tanka poet Fumiko Nakajo) and The Wandering Princess (1960, from the memoir of Hiro Saga, wife of Pujie, brother of Puyi); her films place women at the forefront

items.notes: Arts (film). Profile: the key generalizes the two examples (a woman poet, a noblewoman) into films centered on women's lives, which Film at Lincoln Center's retrospective note also states.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Armando Palacio Valdés’s 1899 novel The Joy of Captain Ribot (translated by Minna Caroline Smith in 1900). The narrator, Julian Ribot, is the captain of a steamship called the Urano.

In Malaga they cook [tripe] not at all badly; in Vigo better yet; in Bilbao I have eaten it deliciously seasoned on more than one occasion. But there is no comparison between any of these, or the way I have had it served in any of the other ports where I have been wont to touch, and the cooking of a Senora Ramona in a certain shop for wines and edibles called El Cometa, situated on the wharf at Gijon.

Therefore, when that most intelligent woman hears that the Urano has entered port, she begins to get her stewpans ready for my reception.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: The narrator explains why he prefers the tripe served in Bilbao to the tripe served anywhere else.
The narrator complains that Senora Ramona rarely has his favorite dish ready when his ship arrives.
The narrator describes the many ports he has visited over the years and the dish for which each of those ports is best known.
The narrator claims that no other port can match one cook’s tripe, and he notes that she prepares for his visits.
items.explanation: The narrator lists ports where tripe is cooked well but says there is “no comparison” between any of them and Senora Ramona’s cooking in Gijon. He adds that when she hears his ship has arrived, she “begins to get her stewpans ready.” Choice D states both points.

A.why_wrong: Bilbao is one of the ports the narrator says cannot compare with Senora Ramona’s cooking in Gijon.

B.why_wrong: The narrator says Senora Ramona starts getting ready for him as soon as she hears his ship has entered port.

C.why_wrong: The narrator names a few ports only to compare their tripe with Senora Ramona’s; he does not describe a different dish for each port.

sources.what: Project Gutenberg 38293, The Joy of Captain Ribot by Armando Palacio Valdes, translated by Minna Caroline Smith (New York: Brentano's, 1900), chapter 1; copied exactly except [tripe] for it; Spanish original La alegria del capitan Ribot, 1899

items.notes: Literary prose. The narrator is captain of the Urano (chapter 1: the captain of the Urano). Spellings Malaga, Senora, Gijon as printed in the 1900 translation.

fixes: excerpt checked against Project Gutenberg 38293: exact except the CB-style [tripe] gloss

items.passage: Adult bearded vultures, large scavengers inhabiting mountainous regions of Europe, Africa, and Asia, typically display conspicuous orange plumage on the head, chest, and legs. This coloration is not produced by the birds’ own pigments; instead, the vultures deliberately bathe in water or mud containing iron oxides, staining their feathers. Some researchers hypothesized that the iron oxides protect feathers from degradation by bacteria. But a team led by Antonio Margalida determined that iron-rich soil had no effect on the growth of such bacteria and that pale and orange individuals reproduced equally successfully.
items.stem: Based on the text, what can most reasonably be concluded about the orange coloration of adult bearded vultures?
options: It is likely produced by pigments that the birds begin to make once they reach adulthood.
Whatever advantage it gives the birds probably does not come from protecting their feathers against bacteria.
It likely makes the birds less successful at raising young than pale birds are.
It is likely acquired by accident when the birds search for carcasses in mountain areas where the soil is rich in iron.
items.explanation: The text says some researchers proposed that iron oxides protect the vultures’ feathers from bacteria, but Margalida’s team found that iron-rich soil did not affect the bacteria’s growth and that orange birds bred no better than pale ones. So if the coloring benefits the birds, the benefit most likely lies elsewhere.

A.why_wrong: The text says the color is not produced by the birds’ own pigments but comes from bathing in iron-rich water or mud.

C.why_wrong: The team found that pale and orange individuals reproduced equally successfully.

D.why_wrong: The text says the vultures deliberately bathe in iron-rich water or mud.

sources.what: Margalida et al., Cosmetic colouring by Bearded Vultures Gypaetus barbatus: still no evidence for an antibacterial function, PeerJ 2019: colour from iron oxides the birds apply by bathing in ferruginous water; no antibacterial effect of ochre on three bacteria; breeding success did not differ between pale and orange birds

items.notes: Natural science (ornithology). P1: an antibacterial function was proposed; P2: no effect on bacteria and no breeding difference; unstated conclusion: any benefit lies elsewhere (the authors favor status signalling, which the passage leaves out).

items.passage: In 1845 HMS Erebus and HMS Terror sailed into the Canadian Arctic on John Franklin’s expedition and never returned. When explorer John Rae relayed Inuit accounts of the crews’ fate in 1854, many in Britain, including the novelist Charles Dickens, dismissed the testimony as unreliable. Yet Inuit knowledge eventually helped guide the discovery of both wrecks: Erebus was found in 2014 near where an Inuk witness had said a ship sank, and Terror was located in 2016 after hunter Sammy Kogvik described seeing a mast protruding from the ice.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Inuit hunters located both of the expedition’s ships many years before British searchers began looking for them.
The expedition’s ships were eventually found through new technology rather than through Inuit accounts.
Inuit accounts of the Franklin expedition, though long dismissed in Britain, proved valuable in finding its ships.
The Franklin expedition failed because its officers ignored advice from the Inuit they encountered.
items.explanation: The text says that in 1854 many in Britain dismissed Inuit testimony about the expedition, yet Inuit knowledge later helped searchers find Erebus in 2014 and Terror in 2016. Choice C states this contrast between the early dismissal and the later value of the accounts.

A.why_wrong: Inuit witnesses described where a ship sank and where a mast was seen, but the text credits the 2014 and 2016 searches with the discoveries.

B.why_wrong: The text says Inuit knowledge helped guide the discovery of both wrecks.

D.why_wrong: The text never explains why the expedition failed or mentions advice the officers ignored.

sources.what: Parks Canada, Inuit traditional knowledge and the Franklin wrecks: Erebus found in 2014 near to where Inukpujijuk told Hall it had sunk; Terror found in Terror Bay in 2016
Sammy Kogvik's sighting of a mast in Terror Bay led to the 2016 discovery; Inuit stories pointed the way for searchers willing to listen

items.notes: History. Rae's 1854 report, based on Inuit testimony, was rejected in Britain, notably by Charles Dickens in Household Words (The Lost Arctic Voyagers, 1854).

items.passage:
The following text is from Hesba Stretton’s 1867 story Jessica’s First Prayer. A man runs a coffee stall in London. He has just asked a hungry girl who has been lingering near his stall why she does not go away.

“I’m just going, sir,” she answered, shrugging her small shoulders to draw her frock up higher about her neck; “only it’s raining cats and dogs outside; and mother’s been away all night, and she took the key with her; and it’s so nice to smell the coffee; and the police has left off worriting me while I’ve been here. He thinks I’m a customer taking my breakfast.” And the child laughed a shrill laugh of mockery at herself and the policeman.
items.stem: According to the text, what is one reason the girl gives for staying near the coffee stall?
options: She enjoys the smell of the coffee that is being served there.
She is waiting for her mother to bring her some breakfast.
She hopes that the policeman will help her find her way home.
She plans to buy some coffee once she has earned some money.
items.explanation: The girl lists several reasons for staying, including that “it’s so nice to smell the coffee.” Choice A restates this reason.

B.why_wrong: The girl says her mother has “been away all night” and took the key; she does not say her mother is coming with breakfast.

C.why_wrong: The girl says the policeman has stopped bothering her because he thinks she is a customer, not that she wants his help.

D.why_wrong: The girl never mentions earning money or buying coffee.

sources.what: Project Gutenberg 50104, Jessica's First Prayer; and, Jessica's Mother by Hesba Stretton, chapter 1 (The Coffee-Stall and its Keeper); copied exactly. Jessica's First Prayer was published as a book in 1867.

items.notes: Literary explicit detail. The context line paraphrases the keeper's question just before the excerpt (why don't you go away, little girl?). The girl gives four reasons; only one appears among the options.

fixes: excerpt checked against Project Gutenberg 50104: exact

items.passage: In parts of south-central Bangladesh, monsoon floods can leave farmland underwater for months at a time. For generations, farmers there have responded by building floating gardens. They pile water hyacinth, a plant that spreads rapidly across rivers and ponds, into thick rafts called dhap, sometimes laying bamboo on top for stability. Vegetables such as okra and gourds are planted on the rafts, and the decaying plant material serves as compost. In 2015 a United Nations agency formally recognized the practice as an important part of the world’s agricultural heritage.
items.stem: According to the text, why do farmers in parts of Bangladesh build floating gardens?
options: Water hyacinth must be cleared from rivers so that boats can pass.
They want their farms to be recognized by the United Nations.
Okra and gourds cannot grow in the soil of the region.
Their farmland is often flooded for long periods of time.
items.explanation: The text says that monsoon floods can leave farmland underwater for months and that farmers have responded by building floating gardens. Choice D states this reason.

A.why_wrong: The text says water hyacinth is used to build the rafts; it never mentions clearing rivers for boats.

B.why_wrong: The United Nations recognized the practice in 2015, long after farmers began using it, so recognition was not their reason.

C.why_wrong: The text says nothing about whether these vegetables can grow in the region’s soil; the problem it names is flooding.

sources.what: FAO GIAHS, Floating Garden Agricultural Practices, Bangladesh (GIAHS since 2015): Gopalganj, Pirojpur and Barisal in south-central Bangladesh, where flood water remains for a long time; floating beds (dhap) of water hyacinth with bamboo; upper layers serve as compost; okra, ribbed gourd and other vegetables

items.notes: Technology and agriculture (traditional farming). Local names include dhap and baira; the passage uses dhap, the name on the FAO page.

items.passage: In 1827 Samuel Cornish, a Presbyterian minister, and John Russwurm, one of the first African Americans to graduate from a US college, founded Freedom’s Journal in New York City. It was the first newspaper in the United States owned and operated by African Americans. At the time, many white-owned newspapers published insulting and inaccurate stories about Black Americans. In the first issue, the editors explained their purpose: “We wish to plead our own cause. Too long have others spoken for us.” The weekly publication also featured news, editorials, and poetry.
items.stem: According to the text, why did Cornish and Russwurm found Freedom’s Journal?
options: They wanted to report news about the college that Russwurm had attended.
They wanted Black Americans to be able to speak for themselves in print.
They hoped to earn money by selling advertisements in New York City.
They planned to reprint stories from white-owned newspapers.
items.explanation: The editors wrote, “We wish to plead our own cause. Too long have others spoken for us,” at a time when white-owned newspapers often misrepresented Black Americans. Choice B restates this purpose.

A.why_wrong: Russwurm’s college degree is mentioned to describe him, not as a subject the newspaper covered.

C.why_wrong: The text never mentions advertisements or earning money.

D.why_wrong: The editors started the paper because others had spoken for Black Americans, often with insulting and inaccurate stories, so they did not plan to reprint those stories.

sources.what: Library of Congress, Freedom's Journal (New York, 1827-1829): founded March 16, 1827 by Samuel Cornish and John B. Russwurm, first African American owned and operated newspaper; editors used it to plead our own cause and oppose misrepresentation in white newspapers

items.notes: History (press history). Cornish was a Presbyterian minister; Russwurm graduated from Bowdoin College in 1826. The opening editorial is quoted exactly.

fixes: loc.gov blocks scripted fetches; core claim confirmed on the Wayback copy of the same page (Cornish and Russwurm, 1827, “to plead our own cause”)

items.passage: Herring gulls in coastal towns frequently snatch food from people. To determine whether the gulls monitor human behavior, Madeleine Goumas and her colleagues placed two identical wrapped snack bars in front of individual gulls. A researcher then picked up one bar and handled it briefly before returning it. Most gulls that pecked at a bar selected the one the researcher had handled. But when the experiment was repeated with sponges instead of snack bars, the gulls displayed no such preference.
items.stem: According to the text, what happened when the researchers used sponges instead of snack bars?
options: The gulls pecked at the sponges more often than at the snack bars.
The gulls chose the sponge that the researcher had touched.
The gulls did not favor the sponge that the researcher had handled.
The gulls flew away as soon as the researcher reached down and picked up a sponge.
items.explanation: The text says that when the test was repeated with sponges, “the gulls displayed no such preference” for the handled object. Choice C restates this result.

A.why_wrong: The text never compares how often gulls pecked at sponges and at snack bars.

B.why_wrong: The gulls favored the handled object only when it was food; with sponges they showed no such preference.

D.why_wrong: The text never says the gulls flew away.

sources.what: Goumas, Boogert and Kelley, Urban herring gulls use human behavioural cues to locate food, Royal Society Open Science 7 (2020): gulls preferentially pecked at the handled one of two identical wrapped flapjacks; with blue sponges of the same size and shape, handling did not draw a preference

items.notes: Natural science (animal behavior). Flapjacks glossed as snack bars. Earlier claim line named Biology Letters; the paper is in Royal Society Open Science.

fixes: listed source (ORE Exeter) unreachable; replaced with the paper on PMC (PMC7062050), which confirms the flapjack and sponge results
explanation quoted “showed no such preference”; the passage says “displayed”, so the quote now matches

items.passage: About 70 circular structures constructed from mammoth bones are known in Ukraine and western Russia. Archaeologists have often described these structures as dwellings occupied for months at a time. Investigating one such structure at a site called Kostenki 11, Alexander Pryor and his team discovered charred wood and seeds inside, indicating that people burned wood as fuel and gathered plants. However, the team found less evidence of activity than a long-term dwelling would leave, suggesting that the structure may have served other purposes.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Archaeologists have found about 70 mammoth-bone structures at the Kostenki 11 site.
People at Kostenki 11 burned mammoth bones because they could not find any wood.
Mammoth-bone structures were built only by people who grew their own crops.
A study suggests that a mammoth-bone structure may not have been a long-term home, as such structures are often thought to be.
items.explanation: The text says that mammoth-bone structures have often been described as long-term homes, but that the team studying the structure at Kostenki 11 found less evidence of activity than a long-term home would leave and suggests it may have served other purposes. Choice D states this main idea.

A.why_wrong: The 70 structures are known across Ukraine and western Russia; the team studied one structure at Kostenki 11.

B.why_wrong: The team found charred wood, which shows that people burned wood for fuel.

C.why_wrong: The text says people gathered plants; it never mentions growing crops.

sources.what: University of Exeter 2020 (Pryor et al., Antiquity): about 70 such structures known in Ukraine and the west Russian Plain; previously thought to be dwellings occupied for months; charred wood, soft plant remains and more than 50 charred seeds found at Kostenki 11; activity less than expected from a long-term base camp

items.notes: Archaeology. Replaces the earlier run's Star Carr subject, which a cross-text item in the same wave also uses.

items.passage: Alston’s singing mice, which inhabit the cloud forests of Central America, communicate using songs composed of many rapid notes. When two mice exchange songs, they take turns. Each mouse begins its song within a fraction of a second after the other stops, much as people do in conversation. Neuroscientists Daniel Okobi, Michael Long, and colleagues discovered that cooling a brain region called the orofacial motor cortex slowed the mice’s songs. When this region was blocked, the mice could still sing but could no longer take turns.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Researchers found that one region of the brain helps singing mice control the timing of their songs as they take turns.
Researchers found that young singing mice learn their songs by listening to older mice.
Alston’s singing mice sing more quickly in cold weather than they do in warm weather.
Alston’s singing mice are the only animals other than humans that take turns when they communicate.
items.explanation: The text explains that singing mice take turns when they sing and that cooling or blocking the orofacial motor cortex slowed their songs or stopped the turn-taking. Choice A states the main finding: this brain region helps the mice time their songs during exchanges.

B.why_wrong: The text never discusses how the mice learn their songs.

C.why_wrong: The researchers cooled a region of the brain, not the air around the mice, and the text says nothing about weather.

D.why_wrong: The text compares the mice’s turn-taking to human conversation but never says no other animals take turns.

sources.what: Okobi, Banerjee, Matheson, Phelps and Long, Motor cortical control of vocal interaction in neotropical singing mice, Science 2019; NYU Langone release: cooling the orofacial motor cortex slowed songs; silencing it left the mice able to sing but unable to take part in vocal exchanges

items.notes: Natural science (neuroscience). Alston's singing mice (Scotinomys teguina) live in cloud forests of Costa Rica and Panama.

items.passage:
The following text is from Mary Louisa Molesworth’s 1882 novel Hoodie. In a family’s nursery, a girl is reading a story aloud. Two small boys are listening.

Into this pretty nursery flies another child—a tiny fairy of a girl, tiny even for her years which are but five—in she flies, down the long passage which leads to the children’s quarters, in at the nursery door, which, in spite of her hurry, she carefully closes, and seeing that the other door is open closes it too, then, flying back to the centre of the room, deliberately sets to work to—children, can you guess?—to scream!

She sheds no tears, there is no grief, only wrath, great and furious, in the little face which should have been so pretty, in the big blue eyes which should have been so sweet.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: A young girl hurries into the nursery to hide from someone who has been chasing her.
A young girl runs into the nursery crying because she has been badly hurt.
A young girl rushes into a quiet nursery and starts screaming in fury.
A young girl interrupts a story because she wants it to be read to her instead.
items.explanation: The text describes a five-year-old girl who flies into the pretty nursery, closes the doors, and “deliberately sets to work to . . . scream.” It adds that there is “no grief, only wrath, great and furious” in her face. Choice C states this main idea.

A.why_wrong: The girl closes the doors carefully, but nothing in the text says anyone is chasing her.

B.why_wrong: The text says she “sheds no tears” and feels “no grief.”

D.why_wrong: The text never says the girl wants to hear the story; she comes in to scream.

sources.what: Hoodie by Mrs. Molesworth, chapter 1 (At War with the World); first published London: G. Routledge, 1882 (archive.org hoodie00molegoog); text copied exactly from the Project Gutenberg 1897 Chambers edition, which matches the 1882 printing for this passage

items.notes: Literary prose. The context line is drawn from the paragraph just before the excerpt (a soft-haired little girl reading aloud to two small boys).

fixes: excerpt checked against Project Gutenberg 26125: exact (the source italicizes scream; the bank carries no italics)

items.passage: Sculptor Augusta Savage moved to New York City in 1921 and gained recognition for portrait busts such as Gamin (around 1929), which depicts a Harlem boy. In 1932 she established the Savage Studio of Arts and Crafts in Harlem. There she instructed young artists, including Jacob Lawrence, who later became a celebrated painter. In 1937 Savage became the first director of the Harlem Community Art Center, which offered free instruction in painting, sculpture, and other arts.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Savage stopped making sculptures after she opened her studio in 1932.
Savage was both an accomplished sculptor and an important teacher of other artists in Harlem.
Savage became well known in Harlem for teaching the young Jacob Lawrence how to make sculptures.
Savage moved to New York City in order to direct the Harlem Community Art Center.
items.explanation: The text describes Savage’s well-known sculptures and then her work teaching young artists at her studio and directing the Harlem Community Art Center. Choice B joins these two parts of her career.

A.why_wrong: The text never says Savage stopped sculpting.

C.why_wrong: The text says Jacob Lawrence became a painter; it does not say she taught him to sculpt or that she was known for this.

D.why_wrong: Savage moved to New York in 1921 and became the center’s director in 1937, so directing it was not why she moved.

sources.what: BlackPast, Augusta Savage (1892-1962): moved to New York 1921; Gamin; opened a Harlem art school in 1932 whose students included Jacob Lawrence; first director of the Harlem Community Art Center in 1937

items.notes: Arts (sculpture, art education). Profile. Gamin, about 1929 (Smithsonian American Art Museum), modeled on a Harlem boy (her nephew).

fixes: blackpast.org blocks scripted fetches; core claim confirmed on the Wayback copy (Gamin, 1932 school with Jacob Lawrence, first director of the Harlem Community Art Center)

items.passage: Insects resting motionless on foliage are acoustically camouflaged from echolocating bats, since a leaf returns a strong echo that obscures the comparatively faint echo of an insect on it. Using a biomimetic sonar device, Inga Geipel and colleagues measured echoes from leaves, with and without insects, from more than 500 angles. Sound striking a leaf nearly head-on produced a strong echo regardless of whether an insect was present, whereas sound arriving at a steep angle was largely deflected elsewhere, much as light is reflected by a mirror. Common big-eared bats hunting in a flight cage approached prey-bearing leaves at such steep angles almost 80 percent of the time.
items.stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about the bats’ steep angles of approach?
options: They likely make an insect’s echo stronger than it would be in a head-on approach, since a leaf struck at a steep angle directs sound toward any insect resting on it.
They likely keep insects from noticing the bats’ calls, since most of the sound that strikes a leaf at such an angle is deflected away from the insect on it.
They likely allow the bats to pick out an insect’s echo, since the leaf beneath the insect then sends little of its own echo back toward the bats.
They likely let the bats locate prey-bearing leaves from farther away, since a leaf deflects sound arriving at a steep angle much as a mirror reflects light.
items.explanation: The text says that a leaf’s strong echo masks the faint echo of an insect on it, that a leaf struck at a steep angle deflects most of the sound away instead of sending it back, and that the bats approached leaves with prey at such angles almost 80 percent of the time. Together these points suggest that the steep approach lets the bats hear the insect’s echo because the leaf’s own echo no longer drowns it out.

A.why_wrong: The text says a leaf struck at a steep angle deflects sound away; it never says the leaf directs sound toward the insect or makes the insect’s echo stronger. What changes is that the leaf’s masking echo is removed.

B.why_wrong: The text never discusses whether insects can hear the bats, and it says sound is deflected away from the bat’s side of the leaf, not away from the insect.

D.recipe: true detail with an unsupported conclusion
D.why_wrong: The deflection is real, but it sends the sound elsewhere instead of back to the bats, so it would not help them find leaves from a distance. What the steep approach does is remove the leaf’s masking echo so that the insect’s echo stands out.

sources.what: Geipel, Steckel, Tschapka et al., Current Biology 2019: leaves mask echoes of silent prey; biomimetic sonar from many angles; leaves act as specular reflectors at oblique angles; wild bats (Micronycteris microtis, common big-eared bat) in a flight cage approached prey from the predicted oblique angles (press accounts: over 500 angles, nearly 80 percent of approaches in the reflecting range)

items.notes: Natural science (sensory ecology). P1: a leaf’s echo masks the insect’s, and a leaf struck at a steep angle deflects sound away; P2: bats approach prey-bearing leaves at those angles; unstated conclusion: the approach removes the masking echo so the insect’s echo stands out. Press figures: 500+ angles, 42 to 78 degrees optimal, almost 80 percent of approaches.

fixes: hardened to band 6: D (head-on approaches confirm prey) fell to the stated head-on fact; now it keeps the true mirror-like deflection and draws an unsupported conclusion (finding leaves from farther away), which fails only once the student sees the deflected sound does not come back; re-solved blind, C only

items.passage: Genetic analyses indicate that the human populations of eastern and southern Africa became separated sometime between about 350,000 and 70,000 years ago. Comparing ostrich eggshell beads excavated at sites across both regions, archaeologists Jennifer Miller and Yiming Wang determined that beads made in southern Africa between about 50,000 and 33,000 years ago closely resembled, in their dimensions and central perforations, those produced some 3,000 kilometers away in eastern Africa. After about 33,000 years ago, the two regions’ bead styles diverged, a change the researchers associate with a climatic shift that brought periodic flooding to the Zambezi River basin, which lies between them.
items.stem: Based on the text, what can most reasonably be concluded about the populations of eastern and southern Africa?
options: They likely remained in contact with each other until a later time than the genetic evidence alone would indicate.
They likely developed their bead-making methods independently, producing similar beads because both relied on ostrich eggshell as a material.
They likely formed a single population until about 33,000 years ago, when flooding in the Zambezi River basin divided them.
They likely began making ostrich eggshell beads in southern Africa before the practice was adopted in eastern Africa.
items.explanation: The bead styles of the two regions matched until about 33,000 years ago and then diverged when flooding disrupted the basin between them, which indicates that the similarity depended on contact across that area. Because the genetic studies place the populations’ divergence between 350,000 and 70,000 years ago, the beads suggest the populations stayed connected well after the genetic evidence alone would indicate.

B.why_wrong: If the two regions had developed similar beads independently, flooding between them would not explain why their styles diverged; the researchers’ link between the flooding and the divergence points to contact, not independent invention.

C.why_wrong: Genetic analyses place the separation of the two populations between about 350,000 and 70,000 years ago. The matching beads point to continued contact between separate populations, not to their being one population until 33,000 years ago.

D.why_wrong: The text never says where ostrich eggshell beads were first made; it only compares beads from the two regions over the same period.

sources.what: Miller and Wang, Nature 2022 (Ostrich eggshell beads reveal 50,000-year-old social network in Africa), abstract: genetic divergence of eastern and southern African lineages about 350 to 70 ka; bead connection about 50 to 33 ka over about 3,000 km; breakdown about 33 ka matching southward ITCZ shift and periodic flooding of the Zambezi catchment; implies a later regional divergence than genetic analyses predict

items.notes: Archaeology. P1: genetic divergence dated 350,000 to 70,000 years ago; P2: bead styles matched until about 33,000 years ago and diverged when flooding cut the connecting basin (so similarity reflects contact); unstated conclusion: contact lasted later than the genetic dates imply (the paper’s own conclusion, left unstated in the passage).

fixes: hardened to band 6: C (stopped making beads) fell to the word diverged; now an overreach that reads the bead contact as one undivided population until 33,000 years ago, killed only by linking it to the genetic separation dates; re-solved blind, A only

items.passage: Engineers Chelsea Heveran, Wil Srubar, and colleagues have developed a building material that is partly alive. They mixed sand and a gelatin-based hydrogel with Synechococcus, a photosynthetic bacterium that toughens the mixture by depositing calcium carbonate, the mineral found in seashells. Because the bacteria live on inside the material, a single block supplied with fresh sand, hydrogel, and nutrients under warm, humid conditions could seed new blocks through three successive generations. The researchers found, however, that the material was strongest when thoroughly dried, and that prolonged dryness sharply reduced the share of its bacteria that survived.
items.stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about a block of the material that has been kept in very dry conditions for a long time?
options: It would likely be stronger than a block kept moist and just as able to seed new blocks, since its bacteria would already have deposited their calcium carbonate.
It would likely regain its full population of living bacteria as soon as it was returned to warm and humid conditions.
It would likely contain less calcium carbonate than the blocks it was used to seed, since each new block draws its minerals from the one before it.
It would likely make a sturdier building component than a block kept moist, but a poorer source of new blocks.
items.explanation: The text says the material is strongest when thoroughly dried, so a block kept dry would be sturdy. It also says that new blocks can be seeded only because the bacteria live on inside the material, and that prolonged dryness sharply reduces how many bacteria survive. A long-dried block would therefore have fewer living bacteria to seed new blocks.

A.why_wrong: The block would likely be stronger, but prolonged dryness kills many of its bacteria, and seeding new blocks depends on living bacteria, so it would not be just as able to seed new ones.

B.why_wrong: The text says regeneration took place under warm, humid conditions with living bacteria, but it never says bacteria killed by dryness recover once moisture returns.

C.recipe: invented comparison with a wrong mechanism
C.why_wrong: The text never compares the calcium carbonate in parent and offspring blocks, and it says new blocks were supplied with fresh sand, hydrogel, and nutrients rather than drawing minerals from the parent.

sources.what: Heveran, Williams, Qiu, Artier, Hubler, Cook, Cameron and Srubar, Matter 2020 (Biomineralization and Successive Regeneration of Engineered Living Building Materials), abstract: sand-hydrogel scaffold inoculated with Synechococcus sp. PCC 7002, toughened by calcium carbonate biomineralization; three successive regenerations from one parent using temperature and humidity switches; structural function maximized at ultradesiccated conditions while prolonged dehydration compromised microbial viability

items.notes: Technology (materials). P1: dry material is strongest; P2: regeneration depends on living bacteria, and prolonged dryness kills them; unstated conclusion: a long-dried block trades regenerative ability for strength. Hydrogel was gelatin-based (press coverage); detail not used by the item.

items.passage: Arguments that games constitute an art form have frequently centered on the narratives games tell or the fictional worlds they depict, effectively treating games as a kind of interactive cinema. Philosopher C. Thi Nguyen locates their artistry elsewhere. A game designer, he observes, determines not only the world of a game but also who the player will be within it, specifying which abilities the player may use, which obstacles stand in the way, and which objectives the player is to pursue. In Nguyen’s view, then, what distinguishes games from the other arts is that their medium is agency itself.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Nguyen argues that games, like films, are art chiefly because of the worlds they depict, though designers also decide which abilities players have within those worlds.
Nguyen contends that games are distinctive among the arts because their designers shape the very capacities and aims with which players act, not just the settings of play.
Although games, like films, often tell stories, Nguyen maintains that the obstacles games present make them more demanding of their audiences than other art forms are.
Nguyen holds that because designers dictate players’ goals and abilities, games restrict players’ freedom in ways that keep games from fully qualifying as art.
items.explanation: The text says that Nguyen looks beyond stories and worlds, arguing that a designer also determines who the player will be: the abilities, obstacles, and goals the player works with. His conclusion is that games stand apart from the other arts because their medium is agency, which is what choice B states.

A.why_wrong: Designers do decide players’ abilities, but Nguyen locates the artistry of games elsewhere than in the worlds they depict; for him, shaping who the player is within the game is the art, not an addition to it.

C.why_wrong: The text mentions obstacles as one thing designers specify, but it never says games are more demanding of their audiences than other art forms.

D.why_wrong: Nguyen treats the designer’s control over goals and abilities as what makes games a distinctive art form, not as something that keeps them from qualifying as art.

sources.what: C. Thi Nguyen, Games: Agency as Art (Oxford University Press, 2020), book abstract: games are a unique art form; designers do not just create a world but who you will be in it, telling you what abilities to use and what goals to take on; games work in the medium of agency

items.notes: Humanities (philosophy of art). Scholar-argument passage like 3.20: a common framing, then the scholar’s alternative, then its conclusion. The opening framing is kept generic (no named holder).

fixes: hardened to band 6: A was the rejected worlds view plus an invented comparison; now a half-true compound (true clause on designers deciding abilities, wrong locus of artistry); re-solved blind, B only

items.passage: Literary scholars have traditionally built their claims on the careful reading of individual works. But as literary historian Franco Moretti observed in 2000, even a specialist in nineteenth-century European fiction really knows only its canonical fraction, which amounts to less than one percent of the novels published; tens of thousands of British novels from that century alone have gone unread, and no one will ever read them all. Since reading more cannot close a gap of that size, Moretti argued, studying literature on a world scale requires a fundamentally different critical method.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Although literary study has long relied on close attention to particular texts, Moretti argued that the vast quantity of unread works demands a different way of studying literature.
Moretti argued that scholars of nineteenth-century fiction should replace the canonical novels they study with lesser-known ones, since the canon represents only a tiny share of what was published.
Moretti contended that nineteenth-century British novels have received far more scholarly attention than novels written in other parts of the world during the same period.
Moretti argued that because the canon is only a tiny share of what was published, the careful reading of individual works no longer has any value for literary scholars.
items.explanation: The text sets the traditional practice of careful reading against Moretti’s observation that the canon is under one percent of published novels and that most novels will never be read. Because reading more cannot close that gap, he argued that a different method is needed, which choice A captures along with the practice it departs from.

B.why_wrong: Moretti argues that reading more cannot solve the problem, so swapping canonical novels for other novels to read would not meet his call for a different method; the text never proposes such a swap.

C.why_wrong: The text mentions British novels only as an example of how many works go unread; it never compares the attention they receive with that given to novels from elsewhere.

D.why_wrong: Moretti says that reading more cannot close the gap and that studying literature on a world scale needs a different method; the text never says that careful reading of individual works has no value.

sources.what: Franco Moretti, Conjectures on World Literature, New Left Review 1 (January to February 2000): he works on the canonical fraction, not even one per cent of published literature; thirty to sixty thousand nineteenth-century British novels no one has read or ever will; reading more is not the solution; world literature asks for a new critical method

items.notes: Humanities (literary history). Two-part main idea with a concession, like 3.21 and 3.16. Moretti’s method (distant reading) left unnamed so the key stays a paraphrase.

fixes: key paraphrased away from the passage wording (close attention to particular texts, a different way of studying literature)
hardened to band 6: D (restrict claims to the canon) was a flat contradiction; now an overstatement that keeps the canon fact and claims careful reading has no value; re-solved blind, A only

items.passage: Through most of the twentieth century, many researchers regarded Amazonia as a largely untouched wilderness, assuming that its early inhabitants had done little to transform the landscape. Work by Umberto Lombardo and colleagues in the Llanos de Moxos, a seasonally flooded savanna in Bolivia, tells a different story. The roughly 4,700 forested islands that dot this otherwise treeless plain turn out to be human-made, the earliest begun about 10,850 years ago, and plant remains preserved in their soils show that squash and manioc were being cultivated there by about 10,250 years ago.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Lombardo and colleagues found that early inhabitants of the Llanos de Moxos cleared much of the forest that once covered the region so that they could grow squash and manioc.
Researchers have concluded that farming in Amazonia began in the Llanos de Moxos and spread from there to other parts of the region over thousands of years.
Because the Llanos de Moxos floods every year, its early inhabitants built forested islands mainly as places to escape rising water rather than as places to farm.
Although Amazonia was long thought to have been little changed by its early inhabitants, evidence from Bolivia shows people reshaping the land and growing crops there over 10,000 years ago.
items.explanation: The text first gives the long-held view that early inhabitants did little to reshape Amazonia, then says Lombardo’s work tells a different story: people built thousands of forested islands starting about 10,850 years ago and grew squash and manioc there by about 10,250 years ago. Choice D states both the earlier view and the evidence that revises it.

A.recipe: twisted detail (creating forest read as clearing it)
A.why_wrong: The text says the forested islands on the plain are human-made, so people created patches of forest rather than clearing one, and it never says the plain was once covered by forest.

B.why_wrong: The text shows early cultivation in the Llanos de Moxos but never says farming in Amazonia began there or spread from there.

C.why_wrong: The text never says why the islands were built, and it says plant remains in their soils show crops were cultivated there, so they were not mainly refuges from water rather than farmland.

sources.what: Lombardo, Iriarte, Hilbert et al., Nature 2020 (Early Holocene crop cultivation and landscape modification in Amazonia), abstract: squash about 10,250 and manioc about 10,350 cal yr BP in the Llanos de Moxos, Bolivia; starting about 10,850 cal yr BP people created about 4,700 artificial forest islands in a treeless, seasonally flooded savannah; humans have altered the Amazonian landscape since their arrival
